displayQuote: Few things help an individual more than to place responsibility upon them

meta.title: Who really said "Few things help an individual more than to place responsibility upon them"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Booker T. Washington wrote it in Up from Slavery (1901), Chapter XI. The original reads “place responsibility upon him… and let him know that you trust him.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Few things help an individual more than to place responsibility upon them'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Booker T. Washington — from Up from Slavery (1901), Ch. XI. The real line ends “…and to let him know that you trust him.”

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1856–1915 · educator, orator & founder of the Tuskegee Institute
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed in Washington’s autobiography Up from Slavery (1901), Chapter XI, where he writes: “Few things help an individual more than to place responsibility upon him, and to let him know that you trust him.” The line reflects on giving Tuskegee students genuine ownership of their school.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: XI — “Making Their Beds Before They Could Lie On Them”

source.excerpt: There are no meetings with our students that I enjoy more than these… These meetings, it seems to me, enable me to get at the very heart of all that concerns the school. “Few things help an individual more than to place responsibility upon him, and to let him know that you trust him. When I have read of labour troubles between employers and employees, I have often thought that many strikes and similar disturbances might be avoided if the employers would cultivate the habit of getting nearer to their employees…”
trail: The line appears verbatim in the Project Gutenberg full text of Up from Slavery: “Few things help an individual more than to place responsibility upon him, and to let him know that you trust him.”
Wikiquote lists it among sourced quotations, citing Up from Slavery (1901), Chapter XI — “Making Their Beds Before They Could Lie On Them.”
The most-shared internet version — “Few things can help an individual more than to place responsibility on him” — softly rewords Washington’s original “Few things help… responsibility upon him.”
source.excerptNote: From Chapter XI, in Washington’s account of how he treated Tuskegee students as co-owners of the institution.

author.heading: About Booker T. Washington
author.metaLine: 1856–1915 · Educator, orator & founder of the Tuskegee Institute
author.bio: Booker T. Washington was born into slavery in Virginia and rose to become the most prominent Black educator and public figure in turn-of-the-century America. In 1881 he founded the Tuskegee Normal and Industrial Institute in Alabama, which he built into a leading school for training Black teachers and tradespeople. His 1901 autobiography Up from Slavery became one of the most widely read American memoirs of its era.

misattribution.heading: A genuine quote — but usually slightly misquoted
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Booker T. Washington is correct and well sourced. What circulates online is usually a lightly reworded version of what he actually wrote.

items.why: Washington’s original sentence reads “Few things help an individual more than to place responsibility upon him”; the popular quote-site version inserts “can” and swaps “upon” for “on” (“Few things can help… responsibility on him”).

The line is almost always quoted without its second half. In the book it continues: “…and to let him know that you trust him,” which is the point Washington was actually making about the Tuskegee students.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought — and very nearly the exact words — are genuinely Washington’s, from Up from Slavery, Chapter XI (1901).

context.heading: Why he wrote it
lead: Washington placed the line in a passage about how he ran the Tuskegee Institute. He describes inviting students, two or three times a year, to write him letters criticizing or making suggestions about the school, and holding “heart-to-heart” chapel talks — his way of making them feel they co-owned the institution rather than merely attended it.

He immediately generalizes the idea to industry, arguing that many “strikes and similar disturbances” between employers and employees could be avoided if employers got “nearer to their employees… and letting them feel that the interests of the two are the same.”
